result: During chronic T. gondii infection (6 weeks post-infection), CD11c+ cells, including cDC1s and cDC2s, accumulate dramatically in the dural meninges around lymphatic vessels near dural sinuses. This accumulation correlates with peak parasite burden in the brain but occurs independently of direct meningeal infection.
evaluation: Claims C2-C8 provide converging evidence from imaging (C2-C4) and flow cytometry (C5-C6) showing significant DC accumulation in meninges during chronic infection. The correlation with brain parasite burden (C7) and absence of meningeal infection (C8) are well-documented with appropriate quantitative methods (PCR, immunostaining, spectral flow cytometry).

result: Chronic brain infection induces differential activation of dendritic cell subsets in the dural meninges, with cDC2s showing broader upregulation of co-stimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86) and MHC class II compared to cDC1s.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figures 1i-k) showing quantitative differences in activation marker expression between cDC1 and cDC2 subsets. The conclusion (C64) appropriately summarizes the differential activation patterns observed in the data.

result: Dendritic cells in the dural meninges actively sample and process CSF-borne protein during chronic infection, as demonstrated by DQ-OVA uptake experiments showing 30% of cDC1s and cDC2s harbor processed antigen within 2 hours, with DQ-OVA+ cells localizing to lymphatic vessels.
evaluation: Claims C13-C15 provide direct experimental evidence using the DQ-OVA tracer system with appropriate time-course analysis. The imaging data (C15, Figure 1m) showing DQ-OVA+ cells in lymphatic vessels supports the inference (C72) that dural APCs capture and transport CSF-borne antigen.

result: CSF-derived protein drains specifically to deep cervical lymph nodes (DCLNs) during chronic infection, where it is sampled by APCs including equal proportions of cDC1s and cDC2s, but not to inguinal lymph nodes (ILNs).
evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are supported by DQ-OVA injection experiments with flow cytometry quantification showing specific drainage to DCLNs but not ILNs. The equal uptake by cDC1s and cDC2s (C18) at both 2h and 24h timepoints provides appropriate temporal resolution.

result: T cell responses in DCLNs peak during chronic infection (6-8 weeks post-infection) and correlate with brain parasite burden, contrasting with ILN responses that peak during acute infection and correlate with peripheral parasite burden.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by longitudinal flow cytometry data tracking both polyclonal (C19) and antigen-specific (C20-C21) T cell responses. The correlation analysis (C22, Figure 2f) appropriately links T cell responses to tissue-specific parasite burden, though the correlation is inferential rather than mechanistically proven.

result: Surgical ligation of lymphatic vessels afferent to DCLNs results in >95% reduction in CSF outflow to DCLNs while preserving drainage to superficial cervical lymph nodes.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by tracer studies using Evans blue and fluorescent ovalbumin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c) with appropriate quantification by fluorescence spectroscopy. The specificity of the ligation (C24) is important for interpreting downstream effects.

result: Meningeal lymphatic ligation reduces CD103+ migratory DC populations and impairs DC maturation in DCLNs without affecting total DC numbers, indicating that lymphatic drainage is required for optimal DC activation during chronic infection.
evaluation: Claims C25-C27 provide complementary evidence: total DC numbers unchanged (C25) but CD103+ subset reduced (C26) and activation markers decreased (C27). This pattern is consistent with impaired DC migration and maturation. The conclusion (C82) is appropriately supported by the data.

result: Restricting meningeal lymphatic drainage by ligation significantly impairs T cell responses in DCLNs, reducing activation (CD69 expression), proliferation (Ki67 expression), and cytokine production (IFN-γ reduced by 60-69%, TNF-α impaired) without affecting total T cell numbers.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 provide comprehensive functional characterization using multiple markers (CD69, Ki67, IFN-γ, TNF-α) with appropriate statistical analysis across multiple experiments (n=9-22 mice). The magnitude of effects is substantial and consistent across assays. The conclusion (C83) appropriately summarizes the findings.

result: Despite impairing T cell responses in DCLNs, meningeal lymphatic ligation has no effect on T cell responses in the brain, including T cell numbers, activation status, cytokine production, or parasite burden, indicating that lymphatic drainage is dispensable for brain immunity during chronic T. gondii infection.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37 provide multiple lines of evidence (total T cells, activation markers, cytokine production, antigen-specific responses, parasite burden) all showing no effect of ligation on brain immunity. This is a surprising negative result that is well-controlled and contrasts with prior work on brain tumors and acute viral infection. The conclusion (C85) is appropriately supported.

result: During chronic infection, antigen-dependent T cell proliferation occurs concurrently in both CNS-draining (DCLNs) and non-CNS-draining (ILNs) lymph nodes, as demonstrated by CellTrace Violet dilution experiments showing 46% and 51% complete dilution in DCLNs and ILNs respectively for OVA-specific T cells.
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by Ki67 staining (C38-C39) and CellTrace Violet dilution experiments (C40-C41) with appropriate antigen-specific controls (Pru-OVA vs parental Pru). The similar magnitude of antigen-dependent proliferation in both lymph node sites (C40-C41) supports the conclusion of concurrent activation (C42, C96).

result: The durability of brain T cell responses after lymphatic ligation is potentially explained by concurrent T cell activation in non-CNS-draining lymph nodes, possibly due to peripheral infection serving to 'immunize' the host or residual antigen persistence after acute infection.
evaluation: Claims C86, C93, and C97 are speculative explanations for the observed data rather than directly tested hypotheses. While the concurrent T cell proliferation in ILNs (C40-C41) provides circumstantial support, the actual source of antigen and mechanism remain unproven. Additional experiments tracking antigen distribution or using tissue-specific infection models would be needed.

result: The accumulation of dendritic cells in dural meninges during chronic infection occurs independently of direct meningeal infection, supporting the concept that immune cells at CNS border tissues respond to brain parenchymal pathology.
evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by the observation that parasite was not detected in meninges (C8) despite DC accumulation. Claim C66 is supported by multiple citations to recent literature establishing this concept. The inference is logical and consistent with emerging understanding of CNS border immunity.

result: The authors propose a model where brain-derived antigen must first reach the CSF before being transported to lymph nodes for T cell activation, contrasting with direct tissue-to-lymph node transport in peripheral organs.
evaluation: Claim C79 is a model inference supported by the experimental findings that: (1) CSF-borne antigen reaches DCLNs (C16-C18), (2) dural DCs sample CSF antigen (C13-C15), and (3) lymphatic ligation impairs DCLN T cell responses (C28-C32). While not directly proven, this model is well-supported by the collective data. Claim C87 appropriately summarizes the main finding.

result: Meningeal lymphatic vessels, which are present in rodents, primates, and humans, drain CSF and immune cells to deep cervical lymph nodes and play important roles in CNS immunity in experimental models of brain cancer and autoimmunity.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C43, C44, C54, C74) are well-supported by citations to established literature (Louveau et al., 2018b; Absinta et al., 2017; Albayram et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020). These represent accurate summaries of prior work that provide essential context for the current study.

result: T. gondii is a brain-tropic pathogen that causes chronic infection requiring continuous T cell responses for host protection, with T cells being actively recruited to the brain and requiring peripheral activation and cognate antigen expression in the brain for persistence.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 accurately summarize established knowledge about T. gondii infection and T cell responses, supported by appropriate citations (Hill and Dubey, 2002; Gazzinelli et al., 1992; Harris et al., 2012; Schaeffer et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2009). This background is essential for contextualizing the study.

result: The dispensability of meningeal lymphatic drainage for T. gondii brain immunity contrasts with its essential role in brain tumor immunity and acute viral infection, potentially due to the presence of peripheral antigen sources during T. gondii infection.
evaluation: Claims C84, C88, and C89 are supported by citations to prior work (Li et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Medawar, 1948). The contrast between these findings and the current study is appropriately highlighted and provides important context for interpreting the results.

result: The authors predict that meningeal lymphatic drainage may not be necessary for immunity against metastatic brain tumors due to early peripheral antigen, and suggest that residual antigen persistence after acute infection likely contributes to T cell proliferation in non-CNS-draining lymph nodes during chronic infection.
evaluation: Claims C91 and C94 are speculative predictions and hypotheses rather than tested conclusions. While they are logical extensions of the data and supported by analogy to other systems (C95), they remain unproven and would require additional experimental validation.

result: The study demonstrates that type 1 and type 2 conventional dendritic cells in the dural meninges undergo significant changes during chronic T. gondii brain infection, including increased numbers, enhanced activation, and ability to sample CSF-borne protein, thereby promoting neuroimmune communication.
evaluation: Claims C73 and C98 are summary statements that accurately synthesize the major findings from multiple experimental approaches (imaging, flow cytometry, DQ-OVA uptake). These conclusions are well-supported by the collective data presented in the manuscript.

result: T cell responses in lymph nodes are parasite-specific rather than due to bystander activation, as demonstrated by lack of cytokine production without antigen stimulation and predominant antigen-dependent proliferation in CellTrace Violet dilution assays.
evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by appropriate negative controls showing no cytokine production without STAg stimulation (Figure 4j, m, p). Claim C106 is supported by comparison of Pru-OVA vs parental Pru showing much greater proliferation with cognate antigen (C40-C41). These controls are essential for interpreting the specificity of responses.

result: OT-I cells detected in brains of Pru-OVA infected mice had completely diluted CellTrace Violet dye, indicating they underwent multiple rounds of proliferation in peripheral lymph nodes prior to brain recruitment.
evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by CellTrace Violet dilution data (Figure 6h) showing complete dye dilution in brain-infiltrating OT-I cells. This is consistent with the established requirement for peripheral T cell activation before brain entry (C50-C51) and provides important validation of the experimental system.
